source.title: Zero-Shot Performance Prediction for Probabilistic Scaling Laws
source.authors: Viktoria Schram; Markus Hiller; Daniel Beck; Trevor Cohn

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a Gaussian-process predictor and Monte Carlo fitting to assess whether held-out learning curves and compute-scaling laws can be predicted; this is a different method from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates held-out nanoGPT loss-curve prediction and predicted compute-scaling laws. Its bilingual and multilingual translation results concern translation-score learning curves, not the claimed language-model pretraining loss laws. Values used to define the hierarchy or choose query strategies are not recorded as outcomes here.
record.test_reason: The study treats the compute scaling law as a given tool. Its results measure how well its Gaussian-process predictor (MaGP) fills in held-out nanoGPT loss curves, and how close a law fitted to predicted plus observed curves comes to the law fitted on all curves. It never tests whether loss follows a power law (V1). It never fits a power law on small runs to predict larger ones (V2), since the held-out curves come from a GP, not an extrapolated power law. It does not vary setup or fitting choices to show exponents shift (V7); the dependence on compute range is only cited from Hoffmann et al. All rows measure the study's own method against baselines or against a full-data reference fit.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that modelling learning-curve datasets as bi-level hierarchies with task correlations (MaGP) improves zero-shot curve prediction across three small NLP datasets, and that the hierarchies are exchangeable. They add that Monte Carlo use of the predictor yields probabilistic scaling laws close to full-data fits at lower cost, and that active learning reduces uncertainty on average.
record.recipe_differences: Uses latent-variable multi-output Gaussian processes and Monte Carlo prediction of missing curves before fitting compute laws, rather than directly fitting scaling laws to a sweep of fully trained models.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that the fitted compute-law form depends on the compute range and subset of learning curves considered. Prediction results also vary with train-test split and with the hierarchy ordering.

fits_no_version.finding: A multi-output GP trained on a subset of nanoGPT loss curves predicts the held-out curves. The predicted slopes are −0.043 (Quad), −0.052 (Tri) and −0.059 (T1), against a reference of −0.056.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Surrogate learning-curve models can recover a compute scaling law from a subset of training runs at reduced cost.

record.code_released: The authors say code for all experiments will be made publicly available; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The scaling-law experiment is limited by computational constraints to 11 sampled points per curve and a five-by-six model grid; training is for one epoch. The study reports prediction-error metrics and AbC but does not test separate parameter- and token-scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations. Reported curves and model range are much narrower than the claim's broad several-orders-of-magnitude scope.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 MAE and MNLPD values were not separately extracted because they follow the reported MSE comparisons; supplementary endpoint tables H.1–H.2, active-learning query-strategy AbC results in Figure 7 and Appendix I, and additional bilingual/multilingual curve-prediction results were also omitted because they do not add direct tests of the stated pretraining-loss power-law claim. The study states that it does not report BNN results for T1small.

untested.parts: Assumes a linear log-log loss-compute law over 10^18–10^20 FLOPs on a 5×6 nanoGPT grid (51M–1.5B). No test of the power-law form or its fit quality, and no parameter or token laws.
No power law is fitted on small runs to predict larger runs; held-out curves are predicted by a GP.
Translation curves (ChrF/BLEU vs dataset size) are predicted with GPs. No power-law form is tested.
No downstream predictability from scale or loss.
Compute-range dependence is cited from Hoffmann et al., not tested. The ground-truth slope differs between the 90-curve set (−0.058) and the 30-curve set (−0.056), but this is not analysed.

record.verdict_notes: This is a methods paper on performance prediction; the scaling law is the target the method reproduces, not the object under test. The reader's V1, V2 and V7 verdicts are withdrawn because every row measures the predictor's error or its agreement with a reference fit. The T1 split does predict the largest models, but via GP interpolation across the architecture grid, not power-law extrapolation.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss scaling with compute only, for a limited nanoGPT setting and a stated compute frontier. Does not test power laws in parameter count or training tokens independently, or establish the claim over several orders of magnitude with other quantities non-bottlenecked.
Tests prediction of held-out nanoGPT configurations in the reported splits, not runs orders of magnitude larger than the training runs.
No fixed-compute sweep to find the loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Translation learning-curve prediction is reported, but the study does not test whether the claimed power-law form holds in those settings or other modalities and training regimes.

The study reports dependence of the compute-law fit on the compute region and the subset of curves used, but does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or demonstrate curves bending away from a single power law.

rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-efficient-frontier law using predicted and observed curves
rows.baseline: Full-data ground-truth law shown in Figure 6: (−0.056c + 3.51)
rows.note: The law is averaged over 10 runs; the authors report the Quad split has the highest AbC.
rows.check: A law fitted to GP-predicted plus observed curves, compared with the full-data reference. It measures predictor fidelity. It does not test the power-law form (assumed linear in log-log, no goodness-of-fit reported) or the effect of fitting choices.

rows.note: Smaller values indicate closer alignment; this is the highest mean AbC among the three reported splits.
rows.check: AbC between the method-derived law and the reference law. This is method fidelity, not a claim measure.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: nanoGPT compute-efficient-frontier fits in the stated compute range
reader_labels.reason: The study fits linear log-log compute laws and reports predicted coefficients for the three splits, supporting this limited compute-only setting; see r19, r21, and r23.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The fitted predicted laws have low reported AbC against the full-data reference, and the authors describe the predicted laws as closely aligned; see r21–r24.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Quad split and reduced nanoGPTsmall dataset
reader_labels.reason: Quad has the highest reported AbC, and reducing the dataset worsens prediction performance; see r19, r20, and r25–r26.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: nanoGPT compute-law fits across the reported splits
reader_labels.reason: The fitted slopes and intercepts vary across train-test splits, and the authors state that the law’s form can depend on the compute range and curves considered; see r19, r21, and r23.
